newsitem.title: GERMANY: German plan for neutrals to join EU defence.
newsitem.headline: German plan for neutrals to join EU defence.

text.p: Germany's Christian Democrats (CDU) unveiled a plan on Monday to let the European Union's non-aligned members join a future common defence policy without having to give up their neutrality.

The plan, meant to bridge the gulf between the 11 NATO countries and the four neutral states within the EU, would let Austria, Finland, Ireland and Sweden have a say in the union's security policy without always having to commit troops to it.

Elmar Brok, a European Parliament deputy and head of the foreign and defence working group for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's party, said the EU could take over all the tasks of the Western European Union (WEU) except collective defence.

Neutral countries have expressed keen interest in taking part in EU peacekeeping missions but needed a way to make this conform with long traditions of standing aloof from NATO, he told journalists in Bonn.
"This is an opportunity we should seize," he said while presenting proposals for the EU's intergovernmental conference (IGC) that he hinted had Kohl's approval.
"This offers them a chance to take part in the common foreign and security policy."

The IGC is now reviewing the 1991 Maastricht Treaty to adjust it before an influx of new members in the next century. Ireland, the current EU president, plans to present a draft of possible treaty reforms at the union's six-monthly summit in Dublin this December.
Brok also said the CDU opposed a French idea for a "Mr or Ms Europe" answerable to the members states who would represent Europe in foreign affairs.

This would allow the EU to organise its own peacekeeping missions along with the neutral countries without forcing them into a NATO-style collective defence as outlined in Article Five of the WEU's treaty.

NATO decided at a June summit in Berlin to back a greater European role in the U.S.-dominated alliance by letting the long-dormant WEU use NATO military equipment in missions Washington does not join.

In the CDU plan, the neutral countries, which originally felt pressured to join NATO to ensure the EU could operate a common foreign and security policy, could decide later whether they wanted to become members of NATO or the WEU.
Brok said majorities in the Finnish, Irish and Swedish parliaments backed this approach while Austria's coalition government had not yet reached a decision on the issue.
He saw support for the idea in other EU countries but admitted it would be difficult to win over Britain, which has long stressed transatlantic unity over European defence plans.
It was essential to keep the issue from polarising positions in the campaign for the British general election due by May next year, he added.
He said Brussels should have a policy coordination unit serving both the European Commission and the member states.
The party, which has frequently stirred up debates within the EU with its strongly pro-European policy papers, also supports majority voting in foreign affairs -- a stand Britain staunchly opposes.

Brok said the EU could write into its treaty almost all of the tasks of the WEU, the 10-nation defence group meant to become the EU's defence arm, but leave its pledge of collective defence for a protocol the neutrals would not have to sign.
